p00937.modern: Thirdly, whereas Bede Beda says, and as the School-men Schoole-men affirm, Paradise to be a place, altogether removed from the knowledge of men( locus a cognitione hominum remotissimus ("a place most remote from the knowledge of men")) and Barcephas conceived, that Paradise was far in the East, but mounted above the Ocean, and all the Earth, and near the Orb of the Moon( which opinion, though the School-men charge Bede withal, yet Pereira Pererius lays it off from Bede upon Strabo Strabus, and his Master Rabanus: ) and whereas Rupertus in his Geography of Paradise, does not much differ from the rest, but finds it seated next or nearest heaven; It may seem, that all these borrowed this doctrine out of Plato, and Plato out of Socrates; but neither of them( as I conceive) well understood: who( undoubtedly) took this place for heaven it self, into which the souls of the blessed were carried after death.

p00938.modern: True it is, that these Philosophers durst not for fear of the Areopagites( in this and many other divine apprehensions) set down what they believed in plain terms, especially Plato: though Socrates in the end suffered death, for acknowledging one only powerful God; and therefore did the Devil himself do him that right, as by an Oracle, to pronounce him the wisest man. Justin Iustine Martyr affirms, that Plato had read the Scriptures; and S. Augustine gave this judgement of him, as his opinion, that( few things changed) he might be counted a Christian. And it seems to me, that both Tertullian and Eusebius conceive, that Socrates, by that place aforesaid, meant the celestial Paradise, and not this of Eden. Solinus, I grant, reports, that there is a place exceeding delightful and healthful, upon the top of Mount Atho( called 〈◊ 〉) which being above all clouds of rain, or other inconvenience, the people( by reason of their many years) are called Macrobioi( that is) Long-lived Long-liued. A further argument is used, for proof of the height of this place, because therein was Enoch preserved from the violence of the Flood floud: approved by Isidore, and Peter Lombard; in which place also Tertullian conceived, that the blessed souls were preserved till the last judgement; which Irenaeus, and Justin Martyr also believed. But this opinion was of all Catholic Divines Diuines reproved, and in the Florentine Council damned; of which S. Augustine more modestly gave this judgement. Sicut certum est ("As it is certain [that they live]") ENOCH & Elijah ELIAM nunc viver: ita ubi nunc sunt, an in Paradiso an alibi, incertum est ("they now live: so where they now are, whether in Paradise or elsewhere, is uncertain"); ( that is) As it is certain that ENOCH and ELIAS do now live: So where they now live, in Paradise or elsewhere, it is uncertain. But Barcephas gives a third cause, though of all other the weakest. For( says he) it was necessary that Paradise should be set at such a distance and height, because the four Rivers Riuers( had they not fallen So precipitate) could not have had sufficient force to have thrust themselves under the great Ocean, and afterwards have forced their passage through the earth, and have risen again in the far distant Regions of India, Egypt Aegypt, and Armenia.

p00940.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 7
p00940.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. VII, sig. 65a
p00940.modern: It is first therefore alleged, that such a place cannot be commodious to live in: for being set So near the Moon, it had been too near the Sun, and other heavenly bodies. Secondly, because it must have been too joint a Neighbour to the Element of fire. Thirdly, because the air in that Region is So violently moved, and carried about with such swiftness, as nothing in that place can consist or have abiding. Fourthly, because the place between the Earth and the Moon( according to Ptolemy Ptolemie and Alfraganus) is seventeen times the Diameter of the Earth, which makes by a gross account about one hundred and twenty thousand miles. Hereupon it must follow, that Paradise, being raised to this height, must have the compass of the whole earth for a Basis & foundation. But had it been So raised, it could hardly be hidden from the knowledge, or eyes of men: seeing it would deprive us of the Suns Sunnes light, all the fore-part of the day, being seated in the East, as they suppose. Now, to fortify the former opinions, Tostatus adds this, that those people which dwell near those falls of waters, are deaf from their infancy, like those which dwell near the Catadupae, or over-falls of Nile Nilus. But this I hold as feigned. For I have seen in the Indies, far greater water-falls, than those of Nile, and yet the people dwelling near them, are not deaf at all. Tostatus( the better to strengthen himself) cites Basil and Ambrose together: to which PERERIVS, Sed ego hac apud ("But I [hold] this among [the opinions];") BASILIVM & AMBROSIVM in eorum scriptis, quae nunc extant, nusquam me legere memini; But I do not remember( says he) that I ever read those things, either in BASIL or AMBROSE.

p00941.modern: But for the bodies of Enoch and Elias, God has disposed of them according to his wisdom. Their taking up might be into the celestial Paradise, for ought we know. For although flesh and blood, subject to corruption, cannot inherit the Kingdom of heaven, and the seed must rot in the ground before it grow, yet we shall not all die( says S. PAVL) but all shall be changed: which change, in Enoch and Elias, was easy to him that is Almighty. But for the rest, the Scriptures are manifest, that by the Flood all perished on the earth, saving eight persons, and therefore in the terrestrial Paradise they could not be.

p00942.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 7
p00942.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. VII, sig. 65a–65b
p00942.modern: For Tostatus his own opinion, who soared not altogether So high as the rest, but believed that Paradise was raised above the middle Region of the air, and twenty cubits above all Mountains Mountaines, that the Flood did not therefore reach it: ( which Scotus and other later School-men also believed; for, say they, there were no sinners in Paradise, and therefore no cause to over-whelm it: ) this is also contrary to the express letter of the Scripture: which directly, and without admitting of any distinction teaches us, that the waters over-flowed all the mountains under heaven. And were it otherwise, then might we as well give credit to Masius Damascenus, and the Thalmudists, who affirm, that there were of the Giants that saved themselves on the Mountain Baris, and on Sion. But to help this, Scotus, being( as the rest of the Schoolmen Schoolemen are) full of distinctions, says; That the waters stood at Paradise, as they did in the Red Sea, and at Jordan; and as the Flood was not natural, So was Paradise saved by miracle. And Thomas Aquinas qualifies this high conceit with this supposition, That it was not believed, that Paradise was So seated, as Bede and others seem to affirm in words, but by Hyperbole and comparatively, for the delicacy and beauty So resembled. But this I dare avow of all those School-men, that though they were exceeding witty, yet they better teach all their Followers to shift, then to resolve, by their distinctions. Wherefore not to stay long in answering this opinion of Tostatus, I confess that it is written, that the Mountains of Olympus, Atho, and Atlas, over-reach and surmount all winds and clouds, and that( notwithstanding) there is found on the heads of the Hills both springs and fruits; and the Pagan Priests, sacrificing on these Mountain tops, do not find the ashes( remaining of their sacrifices) blown thence, nor thence washed off by rains, when they return: yet experience has resolved us, that these reports are fabulous, and Pliny Plinie himself( who was not sparing in the report of wonders) avows the contrary. But were it granted, yet the height of these Mountains is far under the supposed place of Paradise; and on these self Hills the air is So thin( says S. Augustine, whom herein I mistrust) that it is not sufficient to bear up the body of a bird, having therein no feeling of her wings, or any sensible resistance of air to mount her self by.

p00944.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 8
p00944.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. VIII, sig. 65b–66a
p00944.modern: Those which come nearer unto reason, find Paradise under the Aequinoctiall line, as Tertullian, Bonaventure, and Durandus: judging, that thereunder might be found most pleasure, and the greatest fertility of soil: but against it Thomas Aquinas objects the distemperate heat, which he supposes to be in all places So directly under the Sun; but this is ( non causa pro causa ("(not cause for cause")) for although Paradise could not be under the line, because Eden is far from it, in which Paradise was; and because there is no part of Euphrates, Tigris, or Ganges under it, ( Ganges being one of the four Rivers Riuers, as they suppose) yet this conceit of distemper, ( being but an old opinion) is found to be very untrue, though for the conjecture not to be condemned, considering the age when those Fathers wrote, grounded chiefly on this: that whereas it appeared, that every Country, as it lay by degrees nearer the Tropic, and So toward the Aequinoctiall, did So much the more exceed in heat; It was therefore a reasonable conjecture, that those Countries which were situated directly under it, were of a distemper uninhabitable: but it seems that Tertullian conceived better, and So did 〈◊ 〉, for they both thought them habitable enough; and though( perchance) in those days it might be thought a fantastical opinion( as all are which go against the vulgar) yet we now find, that if there be any place upon the earth of that nature, beauty, and delight, that Paradise had, the same must be found within that supposed uninhabitable burnt Zone, or within the Tropicks, and nearest to the line it self. For hereof experience has informed Reason, and Time has made those things apparent, which were hidden and could not by any contemplation be discovered. Indeed it has So pleased God to provide for all living creatures, wherewith he has filled the World, that such inconveniences which we contemplate a-far off, are found by trial and the witness of men's travails, to be So qualified, as there is no portion of the earth made in vain, or as a fruitless lump to fashion out the rest. For, God himself( says ISAY) that formed the earth and made it, he that prepared it, he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited. Now we find that these hottest Regions of the World, seated under the Aequinoctiall line, or near it, are So refreshed with a daily gale of Easterly wind( which the Spaniards call the Breeze, that does evermore blow strongest in the hear of the day, as the down-right beams of the Sun cannot So much master it, that there is any inconvenience or distemperate heat found thereby. Secondly, the nights are So cold, fresh, and equal, by reason of the entire interposition of the earth, as( for those places which my self have seen, near the Line and under it) I know no other part of the World of better, or equal temper: Only there are some tracts, which by accident of high Mountains Mountaynes are barred from this air and fresh wind, and some few sandy parts without trees, which are not therefore So well inhabited as the rest; and such difference of soils we find also in all other parts of the World. But( for the greatest part) those Regions have So many goodly Rivers, Fountains Fountaynes and little Brooks Brookes, abundance of high Cedars, and other stately trees casting shade, So many sorts of delicate fruits, ever bearing, and at all times beautified with blossom and fruit, both green and ripe, as it may of all other parts be best compared to the Paradise of Eden: the boughs and branches are never unclothed and left naked, their sap creeps not under ground into the root, fearing the injury of the frost: neither does Pomona at any times despise her withered husband Vertumnus, in his winter quarters and old age. Therefore are these Countries called Terrae vitiosae; Vicious Countries: for Nature being liberal to all without labour, necessity imposing no industry or travel, idleness brings forth no other fruits then vain thoughts, and licentious pleasures. So that to conclude this part, Tertullian and those of his opinion were not deceived in the nature of the place: but Aquinas, who disliked this opinion, and followed a worse. And( to say the truth) all the School-men Schoole-men were gross in this particular.

p00946.modern: These opinions answered, and the Region of Eden not found in any of those imaginary worlds, nor under Torrida Zona; it follows that now we discover and find out the seat thereof, for in it was Paradise by God planted. The difficulty of which search rests chiefly in this, That as all Nations have often changed names with their Masters; So are most of these places, by Moses remembered, forgotten by those names of all Historians and Geographers, as well ancient as modern.

The Grecians Graecians hated both their Nation and their Religion; and the Romans Romanes despised once to remember them in any of their stories. And as those three Monarchies succeeded each other: So did they transform the names of all those principal Places & Cities in the East: and after them, the Turk Turke has sought( what he could) to extinguish in all things, the ancient memory of those people; which he has subjected and enthralled.

p00948.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 9
p00948.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. IX, sig. 66a–66b
p00948.modern: Now besides those notable marks, Euphrates & Tigris, the better to find the way, which leads to the Country of Eden, we are to take for guides these two considerations( to wit) That it lay Eastward from Canaan & Judaea Iudaeae; and that it was of all other the most beautiful and fertile. First then in respect of situation, the next Country to Judea Iudaea Eastward was Arabia Petraea; but in this Region was Moses himself when he wrote: and the next unto it Eastward also was Arabia the Desert, both which in respect of the infertility could not be Eden, neither have any of the Arabians any such Rivers Riuers, as are expressed to run out of it: So as it follows of necessity, that Eden must be Eastward, and beyond both Arabia Petraea, and Deserta. But because Eden is by Moses named by it self, and by the fertility, and the Rivers only described, we must seek it in other Scriptures, and where it is by the additions of the neighbour Nations better described. In the Prophet Isay I find it coupled and accompanied with other adjacent Countries, in these words, spoken in the person of Sennacherib Senacherib by RABSAKEH: Have the gods of the Nations delivered them, which my Fathers have destroyed, as GOSAN, and HARAN, and RESEPH, and the children of EDEN, which were at Telassar? and in Ezekiel Ezechiel, where he prophesies against the Tyrians: They of Haran, and Calneh Canneh, and Eden, the Merchants of Sheba, Asshur Asbur, and Chilmad, were thy Merchants, &c.

p00949.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 9
p00949.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. IX, sig. 66b–67a
p00949.modern: But to avoid confusion, we must understand that there were two Edens, one of which the Prophet Amos remembers, where he divides Syria into three Provinces Prouinces, whereof, the first he makes Syria Damascene, or Decapolitan: the second part is that Valley called Avenis Auenis, otherwise Conuallis, or the Tract of Hamath Chamath, where Assyria is joined to Arabia the Desert, and where Ptolemy Ptolemie places the City of Averia Aueria: and the third is known by the name of Domus Edenis, or Coelesyria, otherwise Vallis 〈◊ 〉, or the hollow Valley, because the Mountains Mountaynes of Lebanon Libanus and Antilibanus, take all the length of it on both sides, and border it: for Coele in Greek Greeke is Cava in Latine. But this is not that Eden, which we seek: neither does this Province lye East from Canaan, but North, and So joins unto it, as it could not be unknown to the Hebrews. Yet, because there is a little City therein called Paradise, the Jews Iewes believed this Coelesyria to be the same which Moses describes. For the same cause does Hopkins in his Treatise of Paradise reprehend Beroaldo Beroaldus, in that he confounds this Eden, with the other Eden of Paradise: though to give Beroaldo his right, I conceive that he led the way to Hopkins, and to all other later Writers, saving, That he failed in distinguishing these two Regions, both called Eden: and that he altogether misunderstood two of the four Rivers( to wit) Pishon Pison and Gihon Gehon, as shall appear hereafter. Now to find out Eden, which( as Moses teaches us) lay Eastward from the Deserts Desarts, where he wrote, after he had passed the Red Sea; we must consider where those other Countries are found, which the Prophet Isay and Ezekiel joins with it. For( says Isaiah ESAIAH) Gosan, Haran, and Reseph, and the children of Eden, which were at Telassar. Ezekiel in the description of the magnificence of Tyre, and of the exceeding trade that it had with all the Nations of the East, as the only Mart-town Mart-towne of that part of the World, recites both the people, with whom they had commerce, and also what commodities every Country yielded: and having counted the several People and Countries, he adds the particular trade, which each of them exercised: They were thy Merchants( says the Prophet) in all sorts of things, in garments of blue silk, and of embroidered works, fine linen, corral and pearl: and afterwards speaking of the Merchants of Sheba and Raamah, and what kinds they traded, he has these words: The Merchants of Sheba and Raamah were thy Merchants, they occupied in thy Fayres, with the chief of all Spices, and with all precious stones and gold. Now these be indeed the riches which Persia and Arabia Felix Foelix yield: and because Sheba and Raamah Raama are those parts of Arabia, which border the Sea, called the Persian Gulf, therefore did those Nations both vent such Spice, sweet Gums Gummes, and Pearls Pearles, as their own Countries yielded, and( withal) having trade with their Neighbours of India, had from them also all sorts of spices, and plenty of gold. Now the Merchants of Calneh, which Ezekiel joins with Eden, inhabited far up the River, and received this trade from Arabia & India, besides those proper commodities which themselves had, and which they received out of Persia, which bordered them. Jerome Hierome understands by Calneh, Seleucia Selencia, which is seated upon Euphrates, where it breaks into four heads, and which took that name from Seleucus, who made thereof a magnificent City. Hierosolymitanus thinks it to be Ctesiphon, but Ctesiphon is seated down low upon Tigris, and Calneh cannot be on that side, I mean on the East-side of Tigris, for then were it out of the Valley of Shinar. Therefore those which take Calneh for Haran Charran, do much mistake it. p00954.modern: But this City Can or Calneh is made manifest by Moses himself, where it is written of Nimrod: And the beginning of his Kingdom was Babel, and 〈◊ 〉, and Acad, and Calneh, in the Land of Sinaar, or Shinar: where Moses shows the first composition position of the Babylonian Empire, and what Cities and People were subject unto Nimrod, all which lay in the said Valley of Shinar or near it; and this Valley of Shinar is that Tract, afterwards called Babylonia and Chaldea, into which also Eden stretches it self. Chaldea, Babylonia, Sinaar, idem sunt ("Chaldea, Babylonia, Shinar are the same [place].")( says COMESTOR. ) Three names of one Country: which Region of Babylonia took name of the 〈◊ 〉 Babel; and the Tower, of the confusion of tongues. And that Shinar was Babylonia, it is proved in the eleventh Chapter of Genesis, in these words: And as they went from the East, they found a Playne in the Land of Shinar, and there they abode: in which Playne Babyton was built( as aforesaid. )

p00955.modern: Now Shinar being Babylonia, and Calneh, in the first beginning of Nimrods greatness, and before he had subdued any strange, or far-off Nations, being 〈◊ 〉 part 〈◊ 〉 his Dominion, and also named by Moses to be in Shinar, it proves, that Calneh joins to Babylonia; which also Ezekiel couples with Eden, and( further) affirms, that those of Eden were also the Merchants, which traded with the Tyrians: and Isaiah in the threats of Sennacherib against Jerusalem Hierusalem( with other Nations that Sennacherib vaunted that his Fathers had destroyed) names the children of Eden which were at Telassar. But before I conclude where Eden itself lies, it is necessary to describe those other Countries, which Ezekiel joins therewith in the places before remembered, as, those of Sheba and Raamah. It is written in Genesis the tenth: Moreover the sons of HAM were CUSH CVSH, &c. And the sons of CUSH were SEBA, and HAVILAH, and SABTAH. & RAAMAH, &c. And the sons of RAAMAH were SHEBA, & c. and anon after, CUSH begat Nimrod: So as Sheba was the grand child of Cush, and Nimrod the son of Cush, whose elder brother was Sebah: though some there are that conceive to the contrary, that Nimrod was the elder in valour and understanding, though not in time and precedence of birth; who inhabited that part of Shinar, where Babel was built, afterwards Babylonia. His brother Raamah or Regma took that part adjoining to Shinar, toward the Sea side and Persian Gulf( called afterward Raamah and Sheba, by the Father and his Sons, which possessed it. ) For( says Ezekiel) the Merchants of 〈◊ 〉 and Sheba were thy Merchants, they occupied in thy Fair's Faire's with the chief of all spices, and all precious stones, and gold. So as Sheba was that Tract of Country, which parts Arabia Deserta from Arabia Felix, and which joins to the Sea where Tigris and Euphrates fall out, and render themselves to the Ocean. This part, and the confining Country Strabo calls Catabaria, where the best Myrrh and Frankincense is gathered; which people have an interchange or trade with Elana, lying on the East side of the Persian Gulf. By this it appears who were the Shebans Shebeans, spoken of by Ezekiel, and said to have been the Merchants of Tyre, for gold, spices, and precious stones: of which they had not only plenty of their own, but were also furnished from that part of India( called Elana, according to Strabo) for exchange of their Aromatics Aromatiques, and other proper commodities. For as Strabo reports out of ERATOSTHENES: In Persicae 〈◊ 〉 initto Insula est, in qua multi & pretiosi unions gignantur: in alijs vero, clari & 〈◊ 〉 lapilli ("In [illegible] at the beginning of Persia there is an island, in which many precious pearls are produced: but in others, bright [illegible] stones."). ERATOSTHENES( says Strabo STRRBO) affirms, that in the beginning of the Persian Gulf, there is an Island, in which there are many precious pearls bred: and in other, very clear and shining stones. Now, the difference between Sheba, the son of Raamah, and Seba, the son of Cush, is in this, That Seba is written with the Hebrew( Samekh Samech; ) and Sheba with( Shin Schin: ) but whatsoever the difference may be in the Hebrew Orthography, their Countries and habitations are divers. For Sheba is that part which borders the Persian Sea; and Sheba Saba( whence the Queen of Sheba) neighboured the red Sea; and So that place of the 72. Psalm, expounded, Reges Arabum & Sheba, has in the Hebrew this sense: Reges Shebae & Sabae.

And as the Cities of Haran, and Calneh, border Eden on the West and Northwest: So does Sheba on the South, and Chilmad on the North-east. p00958.modern: For it appears both in Isa.. 37. and in the second of Kings, by the threats of Rabsache, the while the Army of Assyria lay before Jerusalem, that the Cities of Gosan, Haran, Reseph, and the Edenites at Telassar, had resisted the Assyrians, though by them( in a sort) mastered and recovered. Have the gods of the Nations delivered them, whom my Fathers have destroyed, as Gosan, and Haran, Reseph, and the children of Eden, which were at Telassar? But it appeared manifestly after Sennacherib's Senacharibs death, that these Nations formerly contending, were then freed from the others subjection: for Esar-Haddon held Assyria, and Merodach Baladan, Babylonia. And after that the Army of Senacharib, commanded by Rabsache, which lay before Jerusalem( Hezekiah Ezechias then reigning) while Senacharib was in Egypt, was by the Angel of God destroyed: the King of Babel sent to Hezekiah, both to congratulate the recovery of his health, and his victory obtained over the Assyrians. After which overthrow, Senacharib himself was slain by his own sons in the Temple of his Idols Idoles, Esar-Haddon succeeding him in Assyria. To the Babylonian Ambassadors Ambassadours sent by Merodach, Hezekiah showed all his treasures, as well proper as consecrate, which invited the Kings of Babylon afterward to undertake their conquest and subversion. So as, the suspicion of 〈◊ 〉 increasing between Babylon and Assyria, the Edenites which inhabited the borders of Shinar towards the North, and towards Assyria, were employed to bear off the incursions of the Assyrians; and their Garrison-place was at Telassar: and the very word( Telassar) says Junius Iunius, signifying as much, as a Bulwark against the Assyrians. This place Hierosolymitanus takes for Resem, others for Seleucia: but this Telassar is the same, which Am. Marcellinus in the History of Julian Iulian( whom he followed in the enterprise of Persia) calls Thilutha in stead of Telassar, who describes the exceeding strength thereof in his 24. Book: It is seated in an Island of Eupbrates upon a steep and unassaultable Rock, in So much as the Emperor Julian durst not attempt it; and therefore it was a convenient place for a Garrison against the Assyrians, being also a passage out of Mesopotamia into Babylonia, and in which the Edenites of the Country adjoining were lodged to defend the same. This place Ptolemy calls Teridata, having Reseph( which he calls Resepha) on the left hand, and Calneh, ( which he calls Thelbe-can) on the right hand, not far from whence is also found the City of Mann-can Mann-canne upon Tigris, and all these seated together, as Isaiah and Ezekiel have sorted them. But the understanding of these places is the more difficult, because Assyria( which the Chaldeans Chaldaeans call Atturia) and Mesopotamia, were So often confounded: the one taken for the other by interchange of Dominion. Assyria & Mesopotamia in Babyloniae nomen transier unt ("Assyria and Mesopotamia passed into the name of Babylonia.")( says NIGER, ) Assyria and Mesopotamia took the name of Babylonia. Lastly, it appears by those adjacent Regions by the Prophets named, in what part of the World Eden is seated, as, by Haran or Haran in Mesopotamia: also by Calneh and Reseph, according to the opinion of Vatablus, who in these words translates this place: Plantaver Plantauer at autem ("But he had planted [a garden];") JEHOVAH Deus hortum in Eden, ab Oriente, The Lord God planted a garden in Eden, Eastward: that is( says he in his Annotations. ) Jusser Iusser at nasci arbors in Eden, Regione Orientali, in finibus Arabiae & Mesopotamiae, He commanded trees to grow in Eden, an Eastern Region in the borders of Arabia and Mesopotamia.

p00960.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 10
p00960.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. X, sig. 68b–69a
p00960.modern: And for a more particular pointing out of this Eden, it seems by the two Epistles of the Nestorian Christians, that inhabit Mesopotamia, which Epistles in the year 1552. they sent to the Pope about the confirming of their Patriarch, and Andraeas Masius has published them, translated out of Syriac into Latine. By these Epistles( I say) it seems we may have some farther light for the proof of that, which we have said about the Region of Eden in those parts. For in them both there is mention of the Island of Eden in the River Tigris, or at least, Tigris in both these Epistles is called the River of Eden. This Island, as Masius in his Preface to these Epistles says, is commonly called Gozoria( as it were, the Island, by an eminence) It has( says he) ten miles in circuit, and was sometimes walled round about, which name of the Island Eden may( doubtless) remain to this day; though in the rest of the Region So called this name be swallowed up, with the fame of those flourishing Kingdoms Kingdomes of Mesopotamia, Assyria, Babylonia, and Chaldea Chaldaea. This Island of Eden has up the River, and not far beyond it, the City of Hasan-Cepha, otherwise Fortis Petra: below it, it has Mosul Mosal or Mosul, from which( as in that which follows it shall appear out of Masius) it is not above twelve miles distant. Neither is it to trouble us, that Mosul or Mosul by Marius Niger is remembered among the Cities higher up Tigris, in these words. Juxta Iuxta autem Tigrim, Civitates Ciuitates sunt Dorbeta prope Taurum montem, quae nunc Mosul dicitur; magna sane, &c ("The Tigris: There are cities, Dorbeta near Mount Taurus, which is now called Mosul; a great [city] indeed, etc.").( that is) By Tigris are these Cities, Dorbeta near unto mount Taurus( which is now called Mosul) which is a great one, &c. This opinion of Niger, displacing Mosul, and making it to be Dorbeta( I say) needs not here to trouble us: seeing for this matter, the testimony of Masius informed by the Christians that dwelt there( the Seat of whose Patriarch it is) ought to be of credit, avowing that this Mosul( or Mozal) is in the confines of Mesopotamia and Assyria, seated upon Tigris, and in the neighbourhood of Nineveh Niniue; and that it is the famous Seleucia Parthorum. The Nestorian Christians in their former Epistle, call it Attur in these words: Ex omnibus Civitatibus Ciuitatibus & pagis quae sunt circum Civitatem Ciuitatem Mozal( hoc est ("that is")) Attur in vicinia Ninives Niniues; Of all the Cities and towns which are about the City of Mozal( that is) Attur in the neighbourhood of Nineveh. As also Niger acknowledges Ctesiphon, a City thereabout to be called Asshur Assur( which is the same as Attur, after the Dialect of those Nations, which change Sh into T.) Neither is it much that he should mistake Ctesiphon( which is not far off Seleucia) for Seleucia, to be Asshur. By this then we may come somewhat near the end of our purpose. For the 〈◊ 〉 of Eden, which lies in the breast of Tigris, is but twelve miles from Mosul, and that ancient City, which Ptolemy Ptolomie and Tacitus call Ninus, and the Scriptures Nineve Nineue, Philostratus, and Simeon Sethi, Mosul, and John Iohn Lean Mosul, others Moss, ( though it be not the same with Mosul) is set but a little higher upon the same river of Tigris, near Mosul: So that we are like to find this Isle of Eden here-about. For the same Andraeas Masius, which places it above Mosul, makes it to be below Hasan chepha, which is upon the same river of Tigris.

p00961.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 10
p00961.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. X, sig. 69a–69b
p00961.modern: The only difficulty is this, that some perhaps may think, that the words of the Nestorians in both their Epistles, speak not of any Isle in Tigris, called the Isle of Eden, but of an Isle in Tigris, a river of Eden. But this sense of their words in my opinion seems the more improbable. And yet if this were the meaning here, we have a testimony from the learned of those parts, that not only Euphrates, but also Tigris was a river of Eden, and that the name of Eden in those parts is not yet quite worn out, though the Region has been subject to the same change, that all other kingdoms of the World have been, and has by conquest, and corruption of other languages, received new and differing names. For the South part of Eden, which stretches over Euphrates, was after the Flood floud called Shinar, and then of the tower of Babel, Babylonia; and the North part of Eden is that Tract of Mesopotamia, Assyria, and Armenia, which embraces both the banks of Tigris, between Mount Taurus, and 〈◊ 〉. And of this Region of Eden. that ancient AETHICUS AETHICVS makes mention, ( not that latter AETHICUS, disciple of CALLINICUS CALLINICVS, otherwise by PLUTARCH PLVTARCH and Athenaeus ATHENAEVS called ISTRI, who lived in Egypt Aegypt in the reign of PHILADELPHUS PHILADEIPHVS, but another of a far higher and remote time) the same being made Latine out of Greek Greeke by S. Jerome HIEROME. And though by corruption of the ancient copy it be written in AETHICUS, Adonis for Edenis; yet Adonis being a river of Phoenicia, cannot be understood to be the Region named by AETHICUS. For AETHICUS makes it a Country, and not a river, and joins it with Mesopotamia and Ethiopia Aethiopia, calling the land of CUSH CHVS Ethiopia, after the Vulgar, and Septuagint. And lastly, the River which waters the Regions( says AETHICUS) falls into the Gulf of Persia: which River he calls Armodius, for Tigris; Tigris being but a name imposed for the swiftness thereof. And out of Armenia both Tigris and Euphrates have their original: for out of Eden came a river, or rivers, to water the Garden, both which Rivers Riuers( to wit) Tigris and Euphrates, come out of Armenia, and both of them traverse Mesopotamia, Regions first of all known by the name of Eden for their beauty and fertility. And it is very probable, that Eden contained also some part of Armenia, and the excellent fertility thereof in divers places, is not unworthy the name of Eden. For in some part thereof( says STRABO) the leaves are always green, and therefore therein a perpetual Spring. Also STEPHANUS STEPHANVS de urbibus ("On Cities") mentions the City of Adana upon Euphrates: and the name of Eden was in use in Amos time, though he speak not of Eden in the East, but of Eden in Coelesyria. But to the end I may not burden the Readers patience with too long a discourse, it may suffice to know, that Euphrates and Tigris( once joined together, and afterward separate) are two of those four heads, into which these Rivers which are said to water the Garden of Paradise, were divided: whose courses being known, Eden, ( out of which they are said to come) cannot be unknown. Now that Hiddekel and Euphrates Perath were Tigris and Euphrates, it is agreed by all: for the Seventy and all others convert Euphrates by Euphrates: & Hiddekel Tigrim omnes exponunt: and all men understand Hiddekel by Tigris( says VATABLE. ) And because that which I have said of the Isle of Eden, shall not be subject to the censure of self-invention, I have here-under set down the words out of the two general Epistles of the Nestorians, as Masius( ad verbum ("Masius (word for word [renders it thus]);")) has converted them into Latine. The occasion of those Letters and Supplications to the Pope were, that the Nestorian Christians which inhabit Mesopotamia, Assyria, Persia, and Babylonia, and have to this day( at least in Queen Mary's Maries time they had) fifteen Churches in one City, called 〈◊ 〉 Parthorum, or Mosul upon the River of Tigris, having no sufficient authority to choose themselves a Patriarch( which cannot be done without four or three Metropolitan Bishops at least) sent to the Bishop of Rome in the year of Christ 1552.( as aforesaid) a Petition to obtain allowance unto such an election as themselves had made: having three hundred year before that upon the like defect, sent one Marius thither to be confirmed; and in this negotiation they made known to the Bishop of Rome the state of the Christian Church in those parts: for upon the death of their Patriarch( who of a covetous desire to enrich himself had forborne to institute Metropolitan Bishops, when the places fell void) they all assembled themselves together to consult of the Church-government Church-gouernment. And because all the Patriarchs for 100. years had been of one house and family to the prejudice of the Church, and that there yet remained one Bishop of the same Stock and Kindred, who aspired to the same dignity, which his Predecessors Predecessours had held, the rest of the Professors Professours refused to allow him. Upon which occasion, and for the choice of a Governor more sufficient, the Teachers in all the Churches assembled themselves. The words of the general Epistle to the Pope are these, about the middle of the said Epistle: Verum nos non acceptavimus neque proclamavimus ipsum, sed subito conuenimus ex omnibus locis Orientalibus, & ex omnibus Civitatibus & Pagis quae sunt circum Civitatem Mosul( hoc est) 〈◊ 〉, in victnia Ninives, ex Babylonia, ex Charrha, ex Arbella, ex Insula quae est in medio Tigris, fluminis Eden, ex Tauris Persiae, ex Nisibi, & c ("But we have neither accepted nor proclaimed him; rather we suddenly assembled from all the eastern places, and from all the cities and villages which are around the city of Mosul (that is) [illegible], in the neighbourhood of Nineveh, from Babylonia, from Harran, from Arbela, from the island which is in the midst of the Tigris, the river Eden, from the Taurus of Persia, from Nisibis, etc."). which is: But we did neither accept of this man, neither pronounced him: but suddenly we assembled our 〈◊ 〉 of all parts of the East, and out of all the Cities and Villages which are about Mosul( or Attur) neighbouring Nineveh, and out of Babylon, Carrhae Carrha, Arbella, and out of the Island which lies in the middle of Tigris, a River of Eden, or rather, out of the Isle of Eden, which lies in the River Tigris. And in a second Epistle at the same time sent, they use these words: Neque supersunt apud nos Metropolitae, quorum est ordinare Catholicum, sed soli pauct Episcopi, Episcopus Arbelae, Episcopus Salmasti, Episcopus Adurbeigan; en e vestigio conuenimus in 〈◊ 〉, quae est intra Tigrim flumen, Eden, fecimusque compactum inter nos, &c.( which is) Neither are there remaining among us any Metropolitan Bishops to whom it belongs to ordain a Patriarch, but only a few Bishops, as the Bishop of Arbela, the Bishop of Salmastus, and the Bishop of Adurbeigan: but lo, we assembled speedily in the Island Eden, which is in Tigris and agreed between our selves, &c.

p00962.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 10
p00962.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. X, sig. 69b–70a
p00962.modern: Now this Island of Eden Masius describes with other places; which being well conceived, the Nestorian Epistles, and the state of the Church may be in those parts( says he) the better understood. And after he has distinguished the four sorts of Christians in those parts of the World, and in the South part of Africa, which he calls Nestorians, Jacobites Iacobites, Maronites Maronitae, and Copts Cophti, he goes on in these words: Mox, 〈◊ 〉 morte, concurrisse aiebant tumultuario in illam quam modo dixi Tigris Insulam, quae duodecim circiter passuum millibus supra Mosul posita, decem fere millia passuum suo ambitu continet, muris undique cincta, & a paucis alijs quam Christianis hominibus habitata ("Soon, [illegible] dead, they said that they had hastily flocked together to that island of the Tigris of which I just spoke, which lies about twelve thousand paces above Mosul, contains almost ten thousand paces in its circuit, is walled all around, and is inhabited by few other than Christian men."): which is, Now hearing of the death of the Patriarch, ( as those that came to Rome reported) they ran tumultuously together into that Island of Tigris or Eden before spoken of, which Island is situated about 12. miles above Mosul, containing very near ten miles in compass, and every where 〈◊ 〉 with a wall, inhabited by a few other men than Christians. And afterward he makes a recapitulation of the Christian Churches; among the rest he adds the Isle of Eden by the name of Geserta, Insula Tigris: sive Geserta. p00963.modern: By this we see that the ancient name of Eden lives, and of that Eden, which lies Eastward from Arabia Petraea, and the Desert where Moses wrote, and that Eden which borders Haran Charran according to Ezekiel Ezechiel, and that Eden which is seated according to the assertion of the said Prophet, and joined with those Nations of Reseph, Calneh Canneh, and Haran, and the rest which traded with the Tyrians, and is found at this day in the parting of the two Regions of Assyria and Babylonia, where the Edenites in Telassar Thelassar were garrisoned to resist the Assyrians, whose displantation Sennacherib Senacherib vaunted of( as above written) and lastly, the same Eden, which embraces Tigris, and looks on Euphrates, two of the known Rivers of those four, which are by all men ascribed to Paradise.

p00965.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 11
p00965.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XI, sig. 70a
p00965.modern: But it may be objected, that it is written in the Text, That a River went out of Eden, and not Rivers, in the Plural, which scruple Matthew Beroaldo Beroaldus has thus answered in his Chronology: The Latine Translation( says he) has these words: Et fluvius egrediebatur de loco voluptatis ad irrigandum Paradisum, qui inde dividebatur in quatuor capita: Quae verba melius consentient cum rei narratione, & eiusdem explicatione, si ita reddantur. Et fluvius erat egrediens ex Edene, ( hoc est ("that is")) 〈◊ 〉 procedebant ex Edene regione ad rigandam pomarium, & inde dividebatur, & 〈◊ 〉 in quatuor capita: which is, And a River went out of the place of pleasure to water Paradise, and thence was divided into four heads: which words( says Beroaldo) do better agree with the narration and explication of the place, if they be thus translated: And a River was going forth of Eden( that is) Rivers went forth, and ran out of the Region of Eden to water the Orchard, and from thence it was divided, and they became four heads. The Tigurine differs from the Vulgar or Latine, for it converts it thus: Et fluvius egrediebatur de delicijs; And a River went out of pleasure, in stead of Eden; and the Latine adds the word locus, or place, Et 〈◊ 〉 egrediebatur de loco voluptatis; And a River went out of the place of pleasure: and So the word( place) may rightly be referred to Eden, which was( of all other) a Region most delightful and fertile; and So also the word( inde) and thence was divided, has reference to the Country of Eden, and not to the Garden it self.

p00966.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 11
p00966.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XI, sig. 70a
p00966.modern: And for the word( River) for Rivers, it is usual among the Hebrews Hebrewes: for it is written: Let the earth bud forth the bud of the herb, that seeds seed, the fruitful tree, &c. Here the Hebrew uses the Singular for the Plural, Herb and Tree, for Herbs and Trees; and again, we eat of the fruit of the tree, in stead of( trees: ) And thirdly, The man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of God; In medio ligni Paradisi; In the middle of the tree of the Garden, for ( trees. ) And of this opinion is David Dauid Kimhi, and Vatablus, who upon this place of Genesis say, that the Hebrews do often put the Singular for the Plural, as illud, for unumquodque illorum ("each one of them"), and he gives an instance in this question it self, as, A River( for Rivers) went out of Eden.

p00967.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 11
p00967.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XI, sig. 70a–70b
p00967.modern: And this answer out of divers of the learned, may, not without good reason, be given to the objection, That Moses speaks but of one River, from which the heads should divide themselves. Howbeit I deny not, but with as good( and perhaps better) reason, we may expound the four heads, to be four notable passages into samous Countries. And So we may take the word( River) Verse the tenth for one River( to wit) Euphrates, as this name comprehends all the branches thereof. For this River, after he is past the place, where we suppose Paradise to have been, divides it self, and ere long yields four notable passages into several Countries, though not all the way down stream, ( for this is no where in the Text) where it is noted, that following the River downward, there is conveyance into the Countries named in the Text, though part of the way to one of the Countries( to wit, to Assyria) were up Tigris.

p00968.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 11
p00968.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XI, sig. 70b
p00968.modern: To this end the Text speaking of Hiddekel, as it rises from the River of Eden, does not say it compasses or washes the whole Region of Assyria, ( as it had used this phrase of Pishon Pison and Gihon Gehon) but that it runs toward Assyria. The first branch Pishon, is Nahar-malcha, ( by interpretation) Basilius, or flumen regium ("the king's river"), which runs into Tigris under Apamia, whence arises the name of Pasi-Tigris, ( as it were) Piso-Tigris. This leads to the Land of Havila Hauila or Susiana. The second branch Gihon, is that which in Historians is Nabarsares, or Narragas, for Nahar-ragas: both which names signify flumen derivatum( a River derived) also 〈◊ 〉, quasi Ranosus, by reason of the froggy Fens Fennes which it makes: this Gihon leads to the first seat of Cush Chus, about the borders of Chaldea Chaldaea and Arabia, and it is lost at length in the Lakes of Chaldea. The third branch, Hiddekel, may be expounded the upper stream of Pishon, or Basilius, which runs into Hiddekel properly So called( that is, into Tigris) above Seleucia, where it shows a passage up Tigris into 〈◊ 〉: where, because at length it is called Hiddekel, or Tigris, having before no known proper name, the Text in this place calls it Hiddekel from the beginning. The fourth Euphrates Perath or Euphrates, So called per excellentiam, being the body of the River Euphrates, which runs through Babylon and Otris. But, be it a River or Rivers, that come out of Eden, seeing that Tigris and Euphrates are noted in the Text, there can be no doubt, but that Paradise was not far from these Rivers: for that Euphrates in Moses is Euphrates, there can be no question; and( indeed) as plain it is that Hiddekel is Tigris. For Hiddekel goes( says Moses) Eastwards towards Asshur Assur, as we find. that Tigris is the River of Assyria proprie dicta, whose chief City was Nineveh Niniue, as in Genesis the tenth it is written: That out of that Land( to wit) Babylonia, Nimrod went into Asshur, and built Nineveh, which was the chief City of Assyria.

p00969.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 11
p00969.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XI, sig. 70b
p00969.modern: And as for the kind of speech here used in the Text, speaking of four heads; though the heads of Rivers be( properly) their Fountains Fountaynes, yet here are they to be understood, to be spoken of the beginning of their division from the first stream. Caput aquae( says ULPIAN VLPIANVS) illud est, unde aqua 〈◊ 〉; siex font nascatur fons; si ex 〈◊ 〉, velex lacu prima initia, &c. If the beginning of the water be out of a Fountayne, then is the Fountayne taken for the head: if out of a Lake, then the Lake; and if from a main River any branch be separate and divided, then where that branch does first bound it self with new banks, there is that part of the River, where the branch forsakes the main stream, called the head of the River.

p00971.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 12
p00971.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XII, sig. 70b–71a
p00971.modern: IT may also be demanded, whether this Region of Eden, by us described, be of such fertility and beauty, as Eden the seat of Paradise was: which if it be denied, then must we also consider, that there was no part of the earth, that retained that fertility and pleasure, that it had before the curse: neither can we ascribe the same fruitfulness to any part of the earth, nor the same virtue to any plant thereon growing, that they had before the Flood floud; and therefore this Region of Eden may be now no such flourishing Country, as it was when it was first created in his perfection. Yet this I find written of it: First in Herodotus, who was an eye-witness, and speaks of the very place it self, for the Isle of Eden is but twelve miles or thereabout from Nineveh Niniue, and So from Mosul Mosal. Ex Euphrate exiens in Tigrim, alterum flumen, juxta quod Urbs Vrbs Ninus sita erat, 〈◊ 〉 regio, omnium quas 〈◊ 〉 〈◊ 〉, optima est, &c. Where Euphrates runs out into Tigris, not far from the place where Ninus is seated, This Region, of all that we have seen, is most excellent; and he adds afterward: Cereris autem fructu procreando 〈◊ 〉 ferax est, utnunquam non fere ducentareddit, &c ("But [the land] is so fertile in producing the fruit of Ceres [illegible] that it almost never returns less than two hundredfold, etc.").( that is) It is So fruitful in bringing forth Corn, that it yields two hundred fold: The leaves of Wheat and Barley being almost four fingers broad: As for the height of Millet and Sesame, they are even in length like unto trees, which although I know to be true, yet I for bear to speak hereof, well knowing, that those things which are reported of this fruitfulness, will seem very incredible to those, which never were in the Country of Babylon. They have commonly in all the Country Palm-trees Palme-trees growing of their own accord, the most of them bearing fruit, out of which they make both meats, and wine, and honey, ordering them as the Fig-trees. Thus far Herodotus.

p00972.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 12
p00972.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XII, sig. 71a
p00972.modern: To this Palm tree So much admired in the East India, Strabo and Niger ad a fourth excellency, which is, that it yields bread; Ex quibus panem, & mel, & vinum, & acetum conficiunt; Of which these people make bread, wine, honey, and vinegar. But Antonius the Eremite finds a 〈◊ 〉 commodity, not inferior to any of those four, which is, that from this self-same Tree there is drawn a kind of fine flax, of which people make their garments, and with which in East India they prepare the cordage for their ships; and that this is true, Athanasius in the life of Antonius the Eremite, confesses, saying: That he received a garment made thereof from the Eremite himself, which he brought with him out of this Region. So therefore those Trees, which the East Indies So highly esteem and So much admire( as indeed the Earth yields no plant comparable to this) those Trees( I say) are in this upper Babylon, or Region of Eden, as common as any Trees of the field. Sunt etiam ("There are also [those who];")( says STRABO) passim per omnem regionem Palmae sua spontenascentes; There are of Palms Palmes over all the whole Region, growing of their own accord. Of this place Quintus Curtius makes this report: Euntibus a 〈◊ 〉 Arabiae odorum fertilitate nobilis, regio campestris interest 〈◊ 〉 Tigrim & Euphratem, jacens tam ubere & pingui solo, ut a pastu repelli pecora dicantur, ne satiet as perimat; ( that is) As you travail on the lest hand of Arabia( famous for plenty of sweet odors) there lies a Champain Country placed between Tigris and Euphrates, and So fruitful and fat a soil, that they are said to drive their Cattle from the pasture, lest they should perish by satiety. Bis in anno segetes Babylonij secant; The Babylonians cut their Corn twice a year( says Niger. ) And as Countries generally are more fruitful to the Southward, then in the Northern parts: So we may judge the excellency of this by that report which Strabo makes of the South part of Armenia, which is the North border of Eden, or a part thereof; his words be these in the Latine: Tota enim haec regio frugibus & arboribus abundat mansuetis, itemque semper virentibus; This Region abounds with pleasant fruits, and trees, always green: which witnesses a perpetual Spring, not found elsewhere but in the Indies only, by reason of the Suns Sunnes neighbourhood, the life and stirrer up of nature in a perpetual activity. In brief, So great is the fertility of the ground, that the people are constrained twice to mow down their Cornfields Cornefields, and a third time to eat them up with sheep: which husbandry the 〈◊ 〉 wanting in the Valley of Mexico, for the first forty years, could not make our kind of Wheat bear seed, but it grew up as high as the trees, and was fruitless. Besides, those fields are altogether without weeds( says Pliny Plinie) who adds this singularity to that soil, That the second year the very stubble( or rather falling down of the seeds again) yields them a harvest of Corn without any further labour: his words are these: Ubertatis Vbertatis tantae sunt, ut sequentianno 〈◊ 〉 restibilis fiat segs ("They are of such fertility that in the following year [illegible] the crop is sown again.").

p00974.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 13
p00974.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XIII, sig. 71b
p00974.modern: After the discovery of Eden, and the testimonies of the fertility thereof, it rests to prove that Pishon and Gihon Gehon are branches of Tigris, and Euphrates. For that the knowledge and certainty of these two Rivers Riuers should trouble So many wise men, it is strange to me, seeing necessity it self( Tigris and Euphrates being known) finds them out: for Euphrates or Tigris, or both be that river or rivers of Eden, which water Paradise, which river or rivers Moses witnesses afterward, divided into four heads, whereof the one is called Pishon, the other Gihon, &c. Could there be a stranger fancy in the World, then when we find both these( namely) Tigris and Euphrates in Assyria and Mesopotamia, to seek the other two in India and Egypt Aegypt, making the one Ganges, and the other Nile Nilus? Two Rivers as far distant, as any of fame known or discovered in the World: the Scriptures making it So plain, that these Rivers were divided into four branches, and with the Scriptures, Nature, Reason and Experience bearing witness. There is no error, which has not some slippery and bad foundation, or some appearance of probability, resembling truth, which when men( who study to be singular) find out, ( straining reason according to their fancies) they then publish to the World matter of contention and jangling: not doubting but in the variable deformity of men's minds, to find some partakers or sectators, the better by their help to nurse and cherish such weak babes, as their own inventions have begotten.

p00975.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 13
p00975.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XIII, sig. 71b–72a
p00975.modern: But this mistaking( and first for the river of Pishon) seems to have grown out of the not-distinguishing of that Region in India, called Havilah, from Havilah, which adjoins to Babylonia, afterward known by the name of Susiana. For Havilah upon Tigris took name from Havilah the son of Cush; and 〈◊ 〉 in India, from Havilah the son of 〈◊ 〉, the one remembered by Moses in the description of Paradise, the other where Moses sets down the generations of Noah, and his sons after the Flood floud. For the sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, and Raamah, and the sons of Joktan Ioctan were Ophir, and Havilah, &c. of which latter( to wit) of Ophir and Havilah the sons of Joktan, that Island of Ophir, ( whence Solomon Salomon had gold) and Havilah adjoining had their names. Now because Ganges is a great and a famous River of the East India, and Havilah a Country of the same, and is situated upon Ganges, hence it came that Ganges was taken for Pishon, which River is said by Moses to 〈◊ 〉 the land of Havilah. Or perhaps it was supposed that those four Rivers, named by Moses, must of necessity be four of the greatest in the World; whence( supposing that Ganges was the next great and famous river after Tigris & Euphrates) they chose out this River to make one of the four. And yet certainly there is another River, whom in these respects they should rather have chosen then Ganges; for the River Indus on this side India, for beauty, for nearness, & for ability, gives no way place to Ganges, but exceeds it in all. And how can any reasonable man conceive, that Ganges can be one of the four heads, seeing Indus comes between it and Tigris? and between Tigris and Indus is all that large Empire of Persia, consisting of many Kingdoms Kingdomes. And 〈◊ 〉, farther toward the East, and beyond Indus, are all those ample Dominions of India within the Ganges Indiaintra Gangem, which lie between those two proud Rivers of Indus and Ganges, now called the Kingdom of Mogor. So as if Indus be not accounted for any of the four, because it is removed from Tigris by all the breadth of Persia, then how much less Ganges, which falls into the Ocean, little less then forty degrees to the Eastward of Indus? Surely whosoever reads the Story of Alexander, shall find, that there is no river in Asia, that can exceed Indus. For Hydaspis was of that breadth and depth, as Alexander thereon in great Galleys Gallies transported himself, and the greatest part of his army, and in sailing down that branch of Indus, found it So large and deep, and by reason thereof So great a billow, as it endangered his whole Fleet, which was ready to be swallowed up therein: Hydaspis( as aforesaid) being but one of many branches of Indus, comparable to it, and as great as it, having besides this, the Rivers of Coas, of 〈◊ 〉, Acesines, Adris, ( otherwise Hirotis, Hispalis, and Zaradrus, all which make but one Indus, and by it are swallowed up with all their children and companions, which being all incorporate and made one stream, it crosses athwart Asia, and then at Cambay Cambaia visits the Ocean Sea.

p00976.modern: But because Pishon, which compasses Havilah, as also Gihon, which waters Cush, must some-where be joined with the rest in one body, or at least be found to proceed out of the same Country of Eden, out of which the other two heads do proceed, out of doubt they cannot either the one or the other, be Ganges, or Nile: for Nile rises in the uttermost of the South, and runs Northward into the Mediterranean Mediterran Sea; and the River Ganges rises out of the mountain Imaus, or( as others will have it) Caucasus, which divides the Northern Scythia from India, and runs from North to South into the Indian Ocean. And as for Euphrates Perath and Hiddekel( that is, Euphrates and Tigris) the one of them is begotten in Armenia, near Georgiana or Iberia, the other not far off in the same Armenia, by the 〈◊ 〉 mountains, So as Ganges, who only travels in her own India, and Nile through Ethiopia Aethiopia and Egypt, never saw the land of Eden, or joined themselves in one Channel, either with themselves, or with either of the other; and therefore could not at any time from thence be separated, or divided into four heads or branches, according to Moses.

p00977.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 13
p00977.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XIII, sig. 72a
p00977.modern: Therefore the River Pishon, which enriches Havilah, is the same which by joining it self with Tigris, was therefore called Pisi-Tigris, or Piso-Tigris, of Pishon and Tigris, which River waters that Havilah, which Havilah the son of Cush gave name unto, and not Havilah of India, So called of Havilah the son of Joktan, who inhabited with his brother Ophir in the East. And this Havilah of the Cushites has also Gold, Bdellium, and the Onyx stone. This Bdellium is a tree, of the bigness, of an Olive, whereof Arabia has great plenty, which yields a certain gum, sweet to smell to, but bitter in taste, called also Bdellium. The Hebrews Hebrewes take the Lodestone for Bdellium. Beroaldo Beroaldus affirms, that Bdela in Hebrew signifies Pearl: So does Eugubinus; and Jerome Hierome calls it Oleaster: be it what it will, a tree bearing gum, or Pearl: Havilah, or Susiana has plenty of both. Now this Country of 〈◊ 〉 or Havilah stretches it self toward the North, as far as the Altars of Hercules, and from thence embraces all that Tract of land Southward, as far as the Persian Gulf, on the East side thereof: from which East side had the Shebans( which traded with the City of Tyre, according to Ezekiel) their great plenty of gold, which Strabo also witnesses, as was showed before.

p00978.modern: The Greeks Greekes had a conceit, that Pishon was Danubius: the Rabbins Rabbines take it for 〈◊ 〉. Aben-Ezra( says Hopkins) out of Rabbi Saadia translates Pishon into Nile: But Nile finds the same impossibility that Ganges does: and Danubius has the Sea of Hellespont and all Asia the less, between it and Tigris. Now Pishon, which runs through Havilah or Susiana, does to this day retain some sign of this name; for where it and Tigris embrace each other under the City of Apamia, there do they agree of a joint and compounded name, and are called Piso-Tigris. And it is strange unto me, that from So great antiquity there should be found remaining any resembling sound of the first name: for Babylon itself, which dwells So near these rivers, is by some writers known by the name of Bandas, as, by Postellus, by Castaldus, of Baldach: by Barius, of Baghdad Bagdad; and of Baghdad, by Andrew Thevet Theuet; and yet all those that have lately seen it, call it Baghdad. To this river of Pishon, Ptolemy Ptolomie indeed with many others give the name of Basilius, or Regius, and Gihon they term Mahar-sares and 〈◊ 〉, and Baarsares. So is Euphrates, near the Spring and fountain, by Strabo and Pliny Plinie called Pixirates: by Junius Iunius, 〈◊ 〉, out of the Hebrew, ( that is) The profusion, or coming forth of Euphrates: where it breaks through the mountain Taurus, it takes the name of Omyra. Plutarch calls it Medus and Zaranda: the Hebrews Parath, ( says Ar. Montanus: ) Pagninus, Euphrates: Josephus Iosephus, Phorah; Eusebius Eusibius, Zosimus Zozimus: Ammianus, Chalymicus: Gistilanus, and Colinutius term it Chebar Cobar: which Ezekiel Ezechiel calls Chebar; but this is but a branch of Euphrates. The Assyrians know it by the name of Armalchar, or Nahor Malcha: but now commonly it is called Frat.

p00980.modern: But Mercer upon Genesis conceives rightly of these rivers: for Euphrates and Tigris( says he) stream into four branches, two of which keep their ancient names, and the other two are called Pishon and Gihon. The reason, why these two rivers joined in one( below Apamia) lose their names, and are called Pisi-Tigris, and the memory of Euphrates extinguished, is, because the best part of Euphrates running through the channel of Gihon, sinks into the Lakes of Chaldea Chaldaea, not far from Ur, the City of Abraham, and fall not entirely into the Persian Sea, as Tigris accompanied with Pishon does.

p00981.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 13
p00981.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XIII, sig. 72b
p00981.modern: This error that Pishon was Ganges, was first broached by Josephus, ( whose fields, though they be fertile, yet are they exceeding full of weeds) and other men( who take his authority to be sufficient in matter of description, whereupon depended no other important consequence) were not curious in the examination thereof. For Epiphanius Epiphantus, Augustine, and Jerome, take this for currant; whereof it followed, that as Pishon was transported into the East India, to find out Havilah: So was Gihon drawn into Africa, to compass Ethiopia. But if Havilah, whereof Muses speaks in the description of Paradise, be found to be a Region, adjoining to Babylon on the one side, and Cush( which is falsely interpreted Ethiopia) fastened to it on the other side, we shall not need then to work wonders( that is) to impose upon men the transportation of rivers, from one end of the World to the other, which( among other uses) were made to transport men. Now it was in the valley of Shinar, where Cush the son of Ham first sate down with his sons Shebah, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, Nimrod, & c. and of Havilah, the son of Cush, did that Region take name, which Pishon compasses; and the land( called Cush) which Gihon waters, took name of Cush himself. For as the sons of Joktan, Ophir and Havilah, seated themselves as near together as they could in India, So did the sons of Cush in Shinar or Babylonia, where Nimrod built Babel: for Havilah or Chavilah Chauilah was first Chusea of Cush; then Chusa, Susa, and 〈◊ 〉.

p00982.modern: From this Havilah unto the Deserts Desarts of Sur, did the Israelites and Amalechites possess all the interjacent Countries: for Saul smote the Amalechites from Havilah to Sur: which Sur, the Chaldean Chaldaean Paraphrast converts Hagra, and Hagra borders the red Sea; but this was not meant from Sur upon the red Sea, to Havilah in the East India, for Saul was no such traveller or Conqueror, and therefore Havilah must be found nearer home, where the sons of Ismael inhabited, and which Country Saul wasted: for Amalek and the Amalechites possessed that neck of Country, between the Persian Sea, and the red Sea; Havilah being the extreme of the one towards the East, and Sur of the other, towards Egypt and the West, leaving that great body of Arabia Felix foelix towards the South, and they spread themselves with the Midianites and Idumeans Edumaeans, from the East part, or back side of the Holy Land, to the banks of Euphrates, comprising the best parts of Arabia Petraea, and Deserta.

p00984.modern: Now, as Havilah Hauilah in the East India drew Pishon Pison So far out of his way thither, So I say did Cush( being by the Seventy translated Ethiopia) force Gihon into Africa. For Cush being taken for Ethiopia by the Greeks Greekes, whom the Latins Latines followed, Gihon consequently was esteemed for Nile Nilus. But Ethiopians Aethiopians are, as much, as black or burnt faces, whose proper Country is called Thebaids Thebaides, lying to the Southward of all Egypt Aegypt. And although there be many other Regions of Ethiopians, and far South in Africa, yet those of Thebaids are those So often remembered in the Egyptian Aegyptian stories, and out of which Nation they had many times their Kings of Egypt: all which 〈◊ 〉 are very near, or else directly under the Equinoctial line, which is very far from that land inhabited by the Cushites Chusites; who are neither black of colour, nor in any sort neighbouring Torrida Zona. But this Translation of the 〈◊ 〉, 〈◊ 〉 does qualify in this manner: There are( says he) two 〈◊ 〉, the East, and the West: and this division he finds in Strabo, out of Homer. Now because there is no colour to make Cush Chush Ethiopia in Africa, Pereira Pererius will make Cush and the Land of the Cushites ( which is Arabia Petraea, and a part of 〈◊ 〉 the Happy, with the Region of Midian Madian) to be the East Ethiopia.

p00985.modern: Now if it be granted, that Cush and the Land of the Cushites, be that Tract from Sur to Havilah, according to the Scriptures: Habitavit Habitauit ISMAEL ab Havilah unto Sur, quae respicit Aegyptum oeuntibus Assyrios ("which faces Egypt for those going to the Assyrians"); ISMAEL dwelt from Havilah unto Sur, that is towards Egypt, as thou go toward Assyria; The same suffices to prove that Gihon cannot be Nile, but a River which waters Cush, and not Ethiopia. But this place of Scripture, Habitavit ISMAEL, & c. has this sense: Ismael dwelt from 〈◊ 〉, which is the way of Assyria, or the Country bordering Assyria; and Sur, which lies toward Egypt, which is as much to say, as, The issues of Ismael( whereof there were twelve Princes) whom God had promised to make a great people, inhabited all those Regions between the border of Egypt and Assyria. And that they were( according to the word of God) So increased and multiplied, it well appeared, when Zearah the Chusite, which others call Tharantha, brought an Army of ten hundred thousand against Asa King of Judah Iuda. Which Army came not out of Ethiopia beyond Egypt; for that had been a strange progress for such a multitude, as ten hundred thousand, having So mighty a King as the King of Egypt, between 〈◊ 〉 and Ethiopia. But these were the Cushites, Amalechites, Midianites Madianites, 〈◊ 〉, and Arabians. For it is written, that after Asa( strengthened by God) had defeated this World of an Army, he in following his victory took some of the Cities of King Zearah round about, as Gerar. Now that Gerar is a City of the Ethiopians, it cannot be suspected: for these be the words of the Scripture disproving it: And ABRAHAM departed thence toward the South Country, and dwelt between Kadesh Cadesh and Sur, and sojourned in Gerar: Now Sur is that part, upon which Moses and the Israelites first set their feet after they passed the Red Sea, where the Amalechites in Rephidim set on them, supposing that they had been weary, and unable to resist. Again, in the story of Isaac it is written: Wherefore ISAAC went to ABIMELECH, and the 〈◊ 〉 unto Gerar: and I am sure Abimelech and the Philistines Philistims were no Ethiopians. And lastly, Moses himself, where he describes the bounds of Canaan, has these words: Then the border of the Canaanites was from Sydon, as thou come to Gerar: for Sydon was the Frontier of Canaan towards the North, and Gerar by Gaza Gazah towards the South. But indeed, howsoever Pereira does with an honest excuse salve his Translation of Cush for Ethiopia, yet it appears plainly, that the Septuagint and Josephus Iosephus did altogether misunderstand this place. And first, for Homers East and West Ethiopia, they are both found elsewhere. For Pliny Plinie in his fifth fift Book and eighth Chapter, cites Homer for an Author, of these two Ethiopia's Aethiopia's. But the East Ethiopia is that which compasses Nile to the South of Egypt, and is the South border thereof; now a part of the Empire of the 〈◊ 〉, under Prester John Iohn; And the West Ethiopia is that, which joins it self with the River Niger, which we call Senegal Senega and Gambia Gambra: for thereabouts are these Ethiopians called Perorsi, Daratites, with divers other names, which Pliny numbers. But all these are in Africa, and beyond the Deserts Desarts thereof, says Pliny out of Homer, Agrippa, and Juba; which Regions indeed( I mean that of Niger, and that of Prester John, and the Troglodytes) lye due East and West. But as for Cush and the Region of the Ishmaelites Ismaelites, & c. they are extended directly North from that Ethiopia, which is beyond Egypt. Now, that Josephus was exceeding gross herein, it appears by that fiction, which he has of Moses when he served Pharaoh Pharao, in the wars against the Ethiopians: for in that( to make Cush, Ethiopia) he transports Midian by miracle over the Red Sea, and beyond all Egypt, and sets it in Ethiopia, as shall be showed more at large in the Chapter of the Worlds Plantation. Again, that Gihon was improperly translated 〈◊ 〉, Pereira confesses, and lays it rather to the corruption of the Greek Greeke Copy, than otherwise. And whereas the Septuagint have converted this place of the Prophet Jeremiah HIEREMIE; And what hast thou now to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Nile? Quidtibi vis in via Aegypti, ut bibas aquam Gihon? to this says PERERIVS, profecto Hebraic ibi non est ("is not") vox Gihon, sed Sichor, quae significat nigrum & turbidum; Truly( says PERERIVS) the word Gihon in this place, is not found in the Hebrew, but Sichor, which signifies black and troubled water.

p00986.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XIV, sig. 73b–74a
p00986.modern: Furthermore, this is a manifest and unanswerable argument, that Cush was ill taken for Ethiopia. Moses married the Daughter of Jethro, Prince and Priest of Midian, whom both the Greek and Latine call a Madianite, and not Aethiopissam, as( with 〈◊ 〉. ) The Geneva converts it, though it help it a little with a marginal note. Now it is without dispute, that Zipporah was of the Country of Midian, which is that part of Arabia Petraea, bordering the Red Sea; for it is written in the second of Exodus, that MOSES fled from Pharaoh into the Land of Midian, and sate down by a Well, & c. and again, in the third of Exodus; when MOSES kept the sheep of JETHRO his father in law, Priest of Midian, &c. Indeed, these four nations are 〈◊ 〉 where mixed in the Scriptures, because they dwell confusedly together( to wit) the Midianites, the Ishmaelites, the Amalekites, and the Cushites, which were all in one general word, Arabians, and in the Scriptures sometimes called by one of those names, and sometimes by another, as in Gen. 37. v. 25. 27. & 28. that Joseph Ioseph was sold to the Ishmaelites; and in the same Chapter, v. 36. it is written, that the Midianites sold Joseph to 〈◊ 〉, Pharaoh's Pharao's Steward. The Genevans Geneuians, in a marginal note( to avoid this confounding of the Nations) say, that Moses wrote according to their opinion, who took the Midianites and Ishmaelites to be all one. But Moses wrote not after any mans opinion, he wrote the truth, and these were all Arabians, and So in this very place it appears by their merchandise, which they brought with them, when they bought Joseph: for their Camels were laden with Spicery and Balm, and Myrrh, which are the Trades of Arabia Felix foelix: from whence chiefly, and from the East India, all the World is served with Myrrh and Frankincense; and their Spices they received from the East side of the Arabian Gulf, as aforesaid. And in the 39. Chapter it is said: That Putiphar bought Joseph of the Ishmaelites, which the Chaldean Chaldaean Paraphrast in the same place calls Arabians. Now, to make this the more manifest, it is written in the sixth sixt of 〈◊ 〉, That when Israel had sown, then came up the Midianites, and the Amalekites, and they of the East, and came upon them: they of the East, were Arabians of the Desert; So as where before in the buying of Joseph, the Midianites and the Ishmaelites were confused, here the Midianites and Amalekites are made one Nation. For in the prosecution of the Story of Gideon Gedeon, the Midianites only are named, as comprehending both Nations; and in the eight Chapter, v. 24. these Nations are all called Ishmaelites, and neither Midianites nor Amalekites. As when Gideon desired, that every man would give him the golden ear-rings, which they had taken after the victory against Zebah and Zalmunna, Kings of Arabia, amounting to 1700. shekels of gold, it is written: For they had golden ear-rings, because they were Ishmaelites. And these Ishmaelites were a great and valiant Nation, and ever in action of war. Manus eius contr 〈◊ 〉, & manus omnium contra eum; His hand( says God of ISMAEL) shall be against all men, and every mans hand against him. Of these Ishmaelites came the Muslim Mahometan Arabians, though some Writers think Mahomet to be of the Schenitae. And these Ishmaelites, which inhabit chiefly in Cedar, and the Deserts of Sur and Paran Pharan( says Josephus) use poison upon their Arrows Arrowes, as the Indians do. Towards the South-east are the Midianites, and Cushites: and beyond them, towards the Deserts of Arabia, the Amalekites; and all are one Nation, and all Arabians.

p00987.modern: Lastly, the ill translation of Ethiopia for Cush, is among other places, made most apparent, in the second of Chronicles, in these words: So the Lord stirred up against Jehoram IEHORAM, the spirit of the Philistines, and the Arabians, which confine the Ethiopians; So Jerome Hierome reads it: the Geneva translation has it, which were besides the 〈◊ 〉 Now, how far it is off between the Philistines, and the Negro's, or the 〈◊ 〉 every man that looks in a Map may judge. For the Philistines and Arabians do mix and join with the Land of the Cushites, and are distant from Ethiopia about two and thirty, or three and thirty degrees, and therefore not their next Neighbours; but all Egypt, and the Deserts of Sur and Paran, are between them. So as this place of the second of Chronicles, should have been translated in these words: So the Lord stirred up against Jehoram, the spirits of the Philistines, and the Arabians, which confine and border upon the Cushites, who indeed are their next Neighbours. * Nulla superest dubitatio quin Ethiopia in Sacris literis sit Arabiae propinqua; There remains no doubt( says Steuchius STEVCHIVS) but Ethiopia in the Scriptures, is taken for that Country, which joins to Arabia.

p00988.section: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. 14
p00988.citation: Book I, Part I, Chapter III, §. XIV, sig. 74a
p00988.modern: Now may we think is it probable, or possible, that Moses could be ignorant of Nile? No, he knew it, no living man So well, and therefore would never have named Gihon, for Nile, or Nile for Gihon. Surely, if Moses had meant Nile, when he named Gihon, he would have called the River( into which he was cast upon Reeds, and preserved by God, working compassion in the Daughter of Pharaoh) a River of Egypt, wherein he was borne and bred, and wrought So many Miracles. Besides, the River of Nile is often named in the Scriptures, but never by the name of Gihon. And if Moses had told the Israelites, that Nile had been a River of Paradise, they might justly have thought, that he had derided them: for they had lived there all days of their lives, and found no such Paradise at all, nor any memory, or speech thereof; except we shall believe the Paradise of Hesperides, where( says Pliny) there was nothing found in his time, but wild Olives Oliues in stead of golden Apples. But Nile is twice called Sichor, once in Isaiah Esay, and once in the Prophet Jeremiah; and yet in those places it is not said to be a River of Ethiopia, but of Egypt. For in a word, the Israelites had never any communion or affairs with the Ethiopians, nor any intelligence, or trade, beyond Egypt, to the South; but the Enemies which they had on the South, and East-parts, were these Nations of the Cushites, Philistines, Ishmaelites, Amalekites, and Midianites: who being often governed by many little Kings, or Reguli, were distinguished in names, according to the Fathers and Heads of those Nations; but in one general name were all Arabians. On the North-side of Canaan, they were afflicted with the Coelesyrians, with the Magogians, Tubalines, and others their adherents; and thirdly within themselves, the Nations, which remained of the ancient 〈◊ 〉, held the strongest Cities upon the Sea-coast( as) Tyre, Sidon, Acre Acon. Gaza, and many others: yea, Jerusalem Hierusalem itself was with-held from Israel( from the days of Moses, even unto the time of David Dauid) by the Jebusites Iebusites.

p00989.modern: That which now remains of most difficulty is, that it does not appear, that any part of Gihon waters that part of Arabia the stony, which the Cushites inhabited in the times of the Kings of Israel: and in this Desert it was that Matt. Beroaldo Beroaldus lost himself in seeking out Paradise: for he was driven( to my understanding) to create two Rivers Riuers, and call them Gihon, and Pishon; to the end that the one might water Cush, and the other Havilah, for I find none such in rerum natura ("in the nature of things"), as he has described: by which Rivers he also includes within Paradise, even Arabia the Arabiathe Desert.
